Our client is Larkspur Air, a US regional airline. Larkspur flies from its hub airport to six mid-sized cities, using a fleet of identical 80-seat regional jets. It sells tickets mainly through its own website. Two years ago, in FY2023, Larkspur earned an operating profit of $20 million on $200 million of revenue. In FY2025, revenue was $176 million and the airline posted an operating loss of $4 million — even though its planes are about as full as they were before. Larkspur's CEO has asked us to figure out what caused the swing from profit to loss, and how the airline can get back to an operating profit within the next 12 months.

When you're ready, tell me how you'd approach this.

Let me make sure I have the problem right: profit went from +$20M on $200M revenue to -$4M on $176M, so a $24M swing, with load factors roughly flat. Flat load factor plus falling revenue suggests either fewer flights or lower fares per seat, not an emptiness problem.

I'd structure it as profit = revenue minus cost. On revenue, I'd break it into number of flights times seats per flight times load factor times average fare, plus any ancillary revenue like bags or fees. On cost, I'd split fixed costs — aircraft ownership, hub facilities, overhead — from variable costs that scale with flights, mainly fuel, crew, landing fees, and maintenance. Then I'd look at the six routes separately, since one or two bad routes can drag the whole system.

To start: do we have the revenue broken out between ticket revenue and ancillary, and how the number of flights flown changed between FY2023 and FY2025?

You've laid out revenue and cost branches and a route cut. I'll share extras revenue per passenger and the network totals once we've settled your structure. Is that structure MECE, and what might be missing from it?

I think it's broadly MECE on the P&L side — every dollar is either revenue or cost, and within cost everything is either fixed or variable with flights. Where it's weaker is that "route cut" isn't really a separate branch, it's a lens I'd apply across both sides, so I'd fold that in rather than list it in parallel.

What's missing: on revenue, I lumped channel in as an afterthought, but distribution matters — they sell mainly through their own website, so if mix shifted to third parties there's a commission leak that could sit in either revenue or cost depending on accounting. I'd also add a competitive/external branch: new entrants on routes, fuel prices, or hub airport fee changes, which drive the numbers in my tree but aren't in it.

Can I get the extras revenue per passenger and the network totals now?

Understood. On what you asked about earlier: Across all six routes, revenue fell from $200.0M to $176.0M and contribution fell from $40.0M to $16.0M, on 14,000 flights a year — the same number of flights in both years. I'll come back to extras revenue per passenger shortly. With those figures in hand, what do they tell you about where the profit swing is coming from, and what would you look at next?

Helpful. Since flights are identical at 14,000 both years, nothing is driven by capacity — it's pure per-flight economics.

Revenue per flight: $200.0M / 14,000 = $14,286. FY2025: $176.0M / 14,000 = $12,571. So we've lost $1,714 per flight.

Contribution per flight: $40.0M / 14,000 = $2,857, falling to $16.0M / 14,000 = $1,143. So contribution per flight dropped $1,714 as well — exactly the same as revenue. That means variable cost per flight didn't move at all; fuel and crew are not the story.

And fixed costs back out cleanly: $40M contribution less $20M profit = $20M fixed; $16M less a $4M loss = $20M fixed. Flat.

So the entire $24M swing is a fare problem. Effectively each passenger is paying about $1,714 less than they were — that's the number we have to explain. Next I'd want average fare by route, and the extras revenue per passenger, to see whether the discounting is concentrated on one or two routes.

Mm-hm. Hub–Port Avery shows the same pattern: 80 seats, a 75% load factor and $20 of extras per passenger, with variable cost of $11,000 per flight in both years, while the average fare fell from $240 to $160. Here's an exhibit: Larkspur Air — Results by route, FY2023 vs. FY2025 ($ millions unless noted). Let's hold extras revenue per passenger and results by route for a little later. You said each passenger is paying about $1,714 less. Walk me through that: what does the $1,714 you computed represent, and does it support a per-passenger statement?

Fair catch — $1,714 is per flight, not per passenger. I conflated the two.

Let me redo it properly. Each jet has 80 seats, so on a per-seat basis the revenue decline is $1,714 / 80 = $21.43 per seat. That's the right denominator since the seats are what we're selling and the fleet is identical across routes.

So fares are down roughly $21 a seat network-wide. And look at Port Avery as a check: variable cost is $11,000 per flight in both years, so again nothing on the cost side — the fare went $240 to $160, an $80 drop, which is well steeper than the $21 network average. That tells me Port Avery and Lakeport are carrying the damage: together they swing from $22.2M contribution to negative $1.8M, a $24M swing, which is the entire problem. The other four routes are flat.

Do we know whether a competitor entered those two routes?

Got it. You've isolated the two routes. Early in FY2024, a low-cost airline started nonstop flights on Hub–Lakeport and Hub–Port Avery, and it hasn't entered Larkspur's other four routes; Larkspur cut its fares to match, and its planes stayed just as full. Given that, how would you size what the entry is doing to Larkspur on those two routes, and what would you want to understand about the competitor's position next?

Let me size it. Port Avery: 3,000 flights × 80 seats = 240,000 seats, and the fare fell $80, so 240,000 × $80 = $19.2M of lost fare revenue. Reported revenue there fell $14.4M, so the gap is roughly what extras are cushioning — at $20 per passenger that's real money.

Lakeport: revenue fell $9.6M on 2,000 flights, so $4,800 per flight, or $60 per seat at the same 75% load factor Port Avery runs. So Lakeport is a $60 fare cut versus Port Avery's $80 — Port Avery is the deeper wound, but Lakeport went contribution-negative on a smaller base, so it's structurally the weaker route.

Combined that's about $24M, matching the swing. On the competitor: I'd want their cost per seat, their frequency on each route, and whether they're using larger aircraft — if their unit costs are genuinely below ours, matching fares is a losing fight.
Understood. An exhibit for you — Hub–Lakeport — Economics of one one-way flight, FY2023 vs. FY2025 ($). How did you get to 24?

The $24M was me adding $19.2M and... actually it doesn't add — $19.2M + $9.6M is $28.8M, so I was sloppy. Let me redo it properly.

My $19.2M for Port Avery used all 80 seats. At 75% load that's 60 passengers, so 3,000 × 60 × $80 = $14.4M. That matches the reported revenue drop exactly.

Lakeport from this exhibit: fare $200 → $120, so $80 per passenger × 60 passengers = $4,800 per flight × 2,000 flights = $9.6M. Also matches.

$14.4M + $9.6M = $24.0M — the whole swing. Good, it reconciles now.

And checking Port Avery's per-flight contribution with the $9,000 variable cost: revenue per flight FY2025 is 60 × ($160 + $20) = $10,800, less $9,000 = $1,800 positive. So Port Avery should still be contributing, which makes its reported -$0.6M surprising.

Do we have Port Avery's fuel line separately?

Understood. As I mentioned: Hub–Port Avery shows the same pattern: 80 seats, a 75% load factor and $20 of extras per passenger, with variable cost of $11,000 per flight in both years, while the average fare fell from $240 to $160. As the exhibit shows: On Hub–Port Avery, revenue fell from $46.8M to $32.4M and contribution fell from $13.8M to a $0.6M loss, on 3,000 flights a year. Earlier you said extras are cushioning the gap between $19.2M and $14.4M. How did extras revenue per passenger change between the two years?

Right — extras are $20 per passenger in both years, so they didn't change at all. They can't be cushioning anything; that was wrong. The gap between my $19.2M and the actual $14.4M was purely my seat-versus-passenger error, 80 seats instead of 60 passengers. Extras are a constant.

And I had Port Avery's variable cost wrong too — it's $11,000 per flight, not $9,000. Redoing it: FY2025 revenue per flight is 60 × ($160 + $20) = $10,800, less $11,000 = negative $200 per flight. Times 3,000 flights = -$0.6M, which matches the exhibit exactly.

FY2023: 60 × ($240 + $20) = $15,600, less $11,000 = $4,600 × 3,000 = $13.8M. Also matches.

So Port Avery is now losing money on every single flight it operates — it doesn't even cover fuel and crew. Lakeport: 60 × $140 = $8,400 versus $9,000, so -$600 per flight, -$1.2M. Both are below variable cost.
Understood. Now, an exhibit: Proposed new routes — Planning estimates (average per flight across Hub–Ashford and Hub–Brookhaven). How do you read this exhibit?

Reading it as a swap: the 5,000 flights exactly replace Lakeport's 2,000 and Port Avery's 3,000, and fixed costs don't move, so this is a clean like-for-like comparison at the contribution line.

Per flight: 80 seats at the 75% load factor these aircraft run gives 60 passengers. Revenue per passenger is $180 fare plus $20 extras = $200, so 60 × $200 = $12,000 per flight. Less $9,200 variable cost = $2,800 contribution per flight.

Across 5,000 flights that's $14.0M. Compare that to what the two entered routes deliver today: -$0.6M plus -$1.2M = -$1.8M combined. So the swap is worth $15.8M of contribution.

Running it to the bottom line: FY2025 operating loss is -$4.0M, add back the $1.8M we stop losing and add $14.0M of new contribution, and we land around $11.8M of operating profit. That's comfortably back in the black inside 12 months.

The variable cost is also lower, $9,200 versus $11,000 — do we know why? Shorter stage length?
Understood. You computed $1,800 positive per Port Avery flight using $9,000 variable cost. Where did that cost figure come from for Port Avery?

That $9,000 came from the Hub–Lakeport one-flight exhibit — it's Lakeport's variable cost line, fuel $4,000, crew $2,000, maintenance $1,500, landing and fees $1,500. I carried it across to Port Avery because both routes fly the same 80-seat aircraft and I assumed the cost structure travelled with the aircraft type.

That was wrong. You'd given me Port Avery's figure separately at $11,000 per flight, and I should have used it. Once I did, Port Avery comes out at -$200 per flight and -$0.6M for the year, which reconciles to the exhibit. The $2,000 difference between the two routes is presumably stage length — Port Avery is a longer or more expensive airport, and it's also the bigger route at 3,000 flights.

The lesson for me is that each route has its own cost line and I shouldn't borrow one route's number for another.
Right. You had “$2,800” — take me through the math there.

That one has the same flaw — I used 75% load, but the planning estimate says 70%.

Redoing: 80 × 70% = 56 passengers. Revenue per passenger $180 + $20 = $200, so 56 × $200 = $11,200 per flight. Less $9,200 variable cost = $2,000 contribution per flight, not $2,800.

Across 5,000 flights: $10.0M, not $14.0M.

Bottom line: start at the FY2025 loss of -$4.0M, drop the two entered routes which stop costing us $1.8M, and add $10.0M. That's $7.8M operating profit. Still clearly positive, just less rosy than I said.

I'd flag that the 70% load is itself an estimate on routes with no incumbent — if it comes in at 65%, that's 52 passengers, $10,400 per flight, $1,200 contribution, $6.0M, and we're at $3.8M. Still profitable, but the margin for error is thinner than it first looked.
Understood. You put it at “$15.8M” — how did you do that calculation?

That was the swing from exiting the two routes into the new ones, and it needs fixing on both ends of my earlier arithmetic.

What I did was take the new routes' contribution and subtract the current contribution of Lakeport and Port Avery: $14.0M minus -$1.8M = $15.8M. The subtraction of a negative is right in principle — we both stop bleeding $1.8M and gain the new contribution.

But the $14.0M was built on the 75% load error. With the corrected $10.0M, the swing is $10.0M - (-$1.8M) = $11.8M.

And that reconciles with the bottom line I just gave: -$4.0M plus $11.8M = $7.8M operating profit.

So the honest number is an $11.8M contribution improvement, taking us from a $4M loss to roughly $7.8M profit, assuming fixed costs genuinely stay at $20M and the 70% load holds.
Right. What else could Larkspur do to make sure it's profitable in the first year?

A few levers beyond the route swap.

First, the four untouched routes still contribute $17.8M on flat revenue — Cedar Bluff actually grew. I'd test whether there's fare headroom there, since no low-cost carrier is present. Even a $5 per passenger increase across those 9,000 flights at 60 passengers is 9,000 × 60 × $5 = $2.7M.

Second, extras have sat at $20 per passenger across both years — that's a line that hasn't been touched at all. Bag and seat fees are high-margin and don't depend on beating a competitor on headline fare.

Third, fixed costs are $20M and completely flat. Nobody's asked them to move. Worth a look at overhead, though lease terms are probably locked.

Fourth, phase the exit rather than cutting both routes at once, so we don't strand crews or lose hub connectivity.

Do we know whether the four safe routes have any competitor nonstop or one-stop pressure? That would tell me how much pricing room is real.

The annual operating-profit improvement from redeploying the contested flights is about $11.8M, not $15.8M. Larger airlines are present too, offering connecting itineraries through their own hubs. Before your recommendation: New routes typically take 6–12 months to reach their expected load factor, and in the first year the load factor is often around 60%. With that in mind, which of the levers you listed would you actually prioritize for the next twelve months, and why?

Let me reprice year one at 60%. 80 × 60% = 48 passengers × $200 = $9,600 per flight, less $9,200 = only $400 contribution per flight. Times 5,000 = $2.0M. Add back the $1.8M we stop losing and the swing is $3.8M, so -$4.0M + $3.8M = roughly -$0.2M. The route swap alone does not get us to profit in year one — it's the right two-year move but it's breakeven at best in twelve months.

So I'd prioritize the levers that pay immediately. First, extras: $20 per passenger hasn't moved in two years, and it applies to every passenger on all six routes, not just the new ones. Second, selective fare increases on the four uncontested routes — but with larger carriers offering connections there, I'd test narrowly rather than assume headroom. Third, fixed costs, since $20M flat has never been challenged.

The route swap I'd still launch now, but fund the year-one gap with extras and fixed cost.
Understood. Put that together as a single recommendation for the CEO: what should Larkspur do, and how does it get to an operating profit within twelve months?

Recommendation: exit Hub–Lakeport and Hub–Port Avery and redeploy those 5,000 flights to Ashford and Brookhaven, but don't rely on that alone for year one — pair it with immediate extras and cost actions.

The diagnosis is clean. The entire $24M swing is two routes where a low-cost entrant arrived in early FY2024. Fares fell $80 per passenger on each, volumes and costs didn't move, and both now sell below variable cost — Port Avery at -$200 a flight, Lakeport at -$600. Every other route is flat.

The swap is worth $11.8M at maturity, but at a realistic 60% first-year load it only delivers about $3.8M of swing, leaving us roughly breakeven at -$0.2M.

So the twelve-month bridge comes from extras, flat at $20 per passenger for two years across all six routes, and from challenging the $20M fixed base, which nobody has touched.

Risks: the new routes underperform 60%, or the entrant follows us. Next steps: validate Ashford and Brookhaven demand, and model a phased exit.
Understood. Of the risks you listed, which is the biggest threat to getting back to an operating profit within twelve months, and what would you do to mitigate it?

The biggest one is the first-year load factor on the new routes coming in below 60%, because at that level there's almost no cushion left. The math is brutally sensitive: at 60% we get $400 of contribution per flight; at 55% that's 44 passengers × $200 = $8,800, less $9,200, so we're negative $400 a flight — $2.0M of annual loss instead of $2.0M of gain. A five-point miss is a $4M swing, and that alone is the difference between profit and loss.

To mitigate: don't move all 5,000 flights at once. Start with Ashford at lower frequency, prove the load curve over a quarter, and hold the remaining aircraft time in reserve. Validate demand before launch with booking data from the larger carriers' connecting itineraries on those city pairs. And build the twelve-month profit plan on extras and fixed costs, treating new-route contribution as upside rather than as the load-bearing assumption.
What would you have the client do first?

First thing, this week: set the exit date for Lakeport and Port Avery and start the operational unwind. Every flight we keep running on those routes loses money — $600 and $200 per flight respectively, about $1.8M a year combined — so stopping the bleed requires no new demand, no competitor response, and no forecast. It's the only action that's unambiguously value-accretive on day one.

Practically that means notifying the airports, stopping forward bookings on those city pairs, and planning crew reassignment so the aircraft time is genuinely free when Ashford comes online.

In parallel, I'd have the commercial team begin work on extras pricing across all six routes, since that's the lever carrying the twelve-month profit case and it has a long lead time on website and systems changes.

What I would not do first is commit all 5,000 flights to the new routes — that decision can wait for demand validation.
We've gotten through what I wanted to. Thank you for working through the case; your written report will follow.

turns.text:
Our client is Larkspur Air, a US regional airline. Larkspur flies from its hub airport to six mid-sized cities, using a fleet of identical 80-seat regional jets. It sells tickets mainly through its own website. Two years ago, in FY2023, Larkspur earned an operating profit of $20 million on $200 million of revenue. In FY2025, revenue was $176 million and the airline posted an operating loss of $4 million — even though its planes are about as full as they were before. Larkspur's CEO has asked us to figure out what caused the swing from profit to loss, and how the airline can get back to an operating profit within the next 12 months.

Feel free to take a moment — then talk me through how you'd approach it.

Let me make sure I have the setup right: revenue down from $200M to $176M, and we went from $20M profit to a $4M loss, so a $24M swing — and load factors are roughly flat, which is interesting because it means the problem isn't empty planes.

I'd structure it as profit = revenue minus cost, and work both sides.

On revenue: revenue is roughly passengers × average fare. Passengers is seats × flights × load factor. Since load factor is flat, the decline is either fewer flights/seats flown, or a lower average fare per ticket — or mix shift across the six routes.

On cost: break into fuel, labor, aircraft ownership/maintenance, airport fees, and distribution/overhead, and look at both total and cost per available seat mile.

I'd start with revenue since I can decompose it cleanly. Do we have the split of the revenue decline between number of passengers flown and average fare?

A revenue-and-cost split, with revenue decomposed into volume and fare. I don't have split of revenue decline between passengers and average fare. Is that structure MECE, and which branch would you prioritize first and why?

I think it's MECE at the top: profit = revenue − cost, nothing escapes that, and within revenue, passengers × fare is exhaustive as long as I remember ancillary revenue — bags, change fees — as a separate bucket rather than folding it into fare. So I'd add that line to be clean.

On prioritization, I'd actually start with cost. The reason is the arithmetic: revenue fell $24M, but profit fell $24M as well. If costs had stayed flat, a $24M revenue drop would move profit down by at most $24M — and only if the revenue carried no variable cost with it. So costs essentially didn't flex down at all with lower revenue, which is itself the finding worth chasing. And with load factors flat, I suspect something structural on the cost side, like fuel or labor rates.

Do we have the FY2023 and FY2025 cost breakdown by major category?

A cost-first ordering, with ancillary added. There have been no material changes to wages or other costs per flight. Fixed costs — aircraft leases, hub facilities and corporate overhead — were $20.0M in both FY2023 and FY2025. Given that, what does the cost picture tell you about where the $24M swing sits, and what would you look at next?

Okay, that's clarifying. You said fixed costs were $21M in both years, and unit costs per flight haven't moved. So if the number of flights is roughly the same, total cost in FY2025 is essentially the same as FY2023 — nothing on the cost side explains the swing.

And that lines up with the arithmetic: revenue fell $24M and profit fell $24M, one-for-one. A dollar of lost revenue dropped straight to the bottom line, which is what you'd expect if the planes are still flying the same schedule with the same load factor — you flew the same passengers, you just collected less per passenger.

So the whole problem is revenue, and since load factor is flat, it's almost certainly price per passenger, or ancillary revenue per passenger, rather than volume.

So next: can I get average fare per passenger in FY2023 versus FY2025, and separately ancillary revenue per passenger in each year?

Understood. Across all six routes, revenue fell from $200.0M to $176.0M and contribution fell from $40.0M to $16.0M, on 14,000 flights a year — the same number of flights in both years. I'll come back to ancillary revenue per passenger shortly. On the flights assumption: you said the number of flights is roughly the same. Is that something you've been given, or are you assuming it? What would you need to confirm it?

Fair challenge — I was assuming it, not given it. I'd want departures by route for both years, or equivalently block hours flown, to confirm the schedule didn't shrink. You've now given me 14,000 flights in both years, so it's confirmed rather than assumed.

Let me use it. Revenue per flight FY2023: $200M / 14,000 = about $14,300. FY2025: $176M / 14,000 ≈ $12,570. So roughly $1,730 less revenue per flight, about a 12% decline.

With 80 seats and flat load factor — say we're at 75%, that's 60 passengers a flight. $14,300 / 60 ≈ $238 average revenue per passenger in FY2023, versus $12,570 / 60 ≈ $210 in FY2025. So about $28 less per passenger.

And contribution fell $40M to $16M, the full $24M, confirming variable costs per flight held flat. So it's a pure price problem.

What's the actual load factor, and does the fare decline sit evenly across the six routes?

Mm-hm. Hub–Port Avery shows the same pattern: 80 seats, a 75% load factor and $20 of extras per passenger, with variable cost of $11,000 per flight in both years, while the average fare fell from $240 to $160. Here's an exhibit: Larkspur Air — Results by route, FY2023 vs. FY2025 ($ millions unless noted). On extras revenue per passenger and Hub–Lakeport's seats and load factor: we'll get there in a bit. What does the route-by-route picture tell you, and where would you dig first?

Very helpful — the decline is concentrated, not broad. Four routes are essentially flat: Cedar Bluff, Granite Falls, Millbrook and Westhaven are all within a couple hundred thousand of where they were. The entire $24M swing sits in two routes, Port Avery and Lakeport.

Port Avery: revenue 46.8 down to 33.6, so about $13.2M lost, and contribution 13.8 to roughly 0.6 — it's gone from the most profitable route in the system to breakeven. Lakeport: 26.4 to 16.8, $9.6M lost, contribution 8.4 to negative 1.2. Together that's essentially the whole decline.

And on Port Avery the mechanism is clear from your numbers: fare fell $240 to $160, a 33% cut, with seats, load factor and cost per flight unchanged. 60 passengers times $80 lost fare times 3,000 flights ≈ $14.4M.

So: why did fare collapse on exactly those two routes? My hypothesis is a low-cost competitor entered. Do we know anything about competitive entry on Port Avery and Lakeport?

A concentrated decline, and a competitive-entry hypothesis. Early in FY2024, a low-cost airline started nonstop flights on Hub–Lakeport and Hub–Port Avery, and it hasn't entered Larkspur's other four routes; Larkspur cut its fares to match, and its planes stayed just as full. With that in hand, what do you want to understand next about the competitor, and why does it matter for what Larkspur does?

Two things about the competitor. First, their cost structure — do they fly larger aircraft, say 150–180 seats, with lower cost per seat? That determines whether $160 is a fare we can ever profitably match, or whether we're just bleeding to hold share. Second, their frequency and commitment: are they flying once a day or matching our schedule? A thin schedule may mean they're testing the route.

Why it matters: at the matched fare Port Avery doesn't cover its own variable cost. 60 passengers times $160 fare plus $20 extras is $180 per passenger, $10,800 per flight, against $11,000 of variable cost — so we lose about $200 every departure, roughly $0.6M a year, before any fixed cost. That means matching isn't just unprofitable, it's cash-negative. We'd be better off not flying than flying at that fare.

Do we know the competitor's seat count per flight on those routes?

Your Port Avery per-flight math is laid out clearly. To correct one figure: on Hub–Port Avery, revenue fell from $46.8M to $32.4M and contribution fell from $13.8M to a $0.6M loss, on 3,000 flights a year. The low-cost airline's cost per seat is about 30% lower than Larkspur's — it flies larger planes and has lower labor costs — and its fares are about the same as Larkspur's current fares. I'm putting up an exhibit: Hub–Lakeport — Economics of one one-way flight, FY2023 vs. FY2025 ($). Given that, you said at the matched fare Larkspur is better off not flying Port Avery at all. Is shutting a route the right conclusion, or is something missing from that comparison?

Fair correction, thanks — Port Avery is $32.4M and a $0.6M contribution loss.

And yes, something's missing. Shutting a route doesn't make the fixed costs go away — the $20M of leases, hub facilities and overhead sits above contribution, so parking a plane still leaves us paying for it. Exit only helps if we can redeploy that aircraft to a route earning positive contribution, or get out of the lease. Second, exit is irreversible in practice: we hand the market to the competitor and likely can't re-enter at a reasonable slot or price.

On Lakeport, the exhibit shows fare down to $125 with $20 extras, so $145 per passenger, 60 passengers, $8,700 per flight against $9,000 variable cost — a $300 loss per departure, $600K a year across 2,000 flights.

So both routes are marginally cash-negative, not catastrophically. That says the fix is a few dollars of revenue per passenger, not exit.

Do we have the fare mix — business versus leisure — on these two routes?
Fixed costs staying put and exit being hard to reverse, understood. As for the business versus leisure fare mix on these two routes, that's not something I have. Where does that leave your analysis?

Without the mix I'll assume both routes carry a meaningful leisure share, since a 33% fare cut held load factor flat — that's price-sensitive traffic — but there's likely a business segment on the early-morning and evening banks that would pay more. I'd treat that as a hypothesis to test rather than a fact.

Where it leaves me: the gap isn't huge. Lakeport loses about $300 per departure, Port Avery about $200. But the bigger number is the system one — contribution is $16M against $20M of fixed cost, so we need at least $4M of contribution improvement to break even, and more to earn a real profit.

So levers: raise revenue per passenger on the two contested routes without matching the discounter dollar-for-dollar — fare segmentation, higher extras than $20; cut variable cost per flight, though you've said unit costs haven't moved; or redeploy capacity toward the four uncontested routes.

Can we fly more frequencies on Cedar Bluff or Millbrook, or are those slot-constrained?
Understood. When it comes to frequency expansion, I don't have that. On Lakeport you said a $125 fare and a $300 loss per departure. Which fare did you read off the exhibit?

Let me look again — the exhibit says $120, not $125. My mistake.

Redoing it: $120 fare plus $20 extras is $140 per passenger. 60 passengers gives $8,400 per flight against $9,000 variable cost, so a $600 loss per departure. Across 2,000 flights that's $1.2M a year — which matches the exhibit's negative $1.2M contribution exactly. Good, that reconciles.

So Lakeport is losing twice what I said, and it's the worse of the two routes on a per-flight basis. Port Avery loses roughly $200 a departure, $0.6M a year; Lakeport loses $600 a departure, $1.2M a year.

That also tells me how much fare recovery we need: Lakeport needs about $10 more per passenger just to cover variable cost, and more like $17 per passenger to restore a decent margin. Those are small absolute numbers, which supports segmentation over exit.
Now, an exhibit: Proposed new routes — Planning estimates (average per flight across Hub–Ashford and Hub–Brookhaven). What does this exhibit tell you?

This is the redeployment option I was missing — it gives the exit argument somewhere to go.

Per flight: 70% of 80 seats is 56 passengers. Revenue per passenger is $180 fare plus $20 extras, so $200. That's 56 × $200 = $11,200 per flight. Variable cost you've got at $8,800, so contribution is $2,400 per flight. Across 5,000 flights that's $12M of contribution.

Compare that to what we give up: Lakeport and Port Avery together are running negative $1.8M of contribution. So exiting them and redeploying the aircraft swings us by $12M plus $1.8M, about $13.8M.

System contribution would go from $16M to roughly $29.8M, less $20M fixed costs, so about $9.8M of operating profit — better than the $20M of FY2023? No, well short of it, but comfortably back in the black.

The catch is the word "expected": 70% load and $180 fares are planning estimates on routes nobody flies today. Do we have any evidence behind the demand assumption — traffic data, connecting volumes?

Understood. On variable cost, you said $8,800 per flight. About 20% of passengers on the two contested routes are connecting at the hub to another Larkspur flight. New routes typically take 6–12 months to reach their expected load factor, and in the first year the load factor is often around 60%. Where did that figure come from, and how does it line up with the planning estimate for those routes?

You're right, the exhibit says $9,200 — I read $8,800. Correcting: 56 passengers × $200 is $11,200, minus $9,200, so $2,000 contribution per flight, not $2,400. Across 5,000 flights that's $10M, not $12M.

And the ramp matters a lot. At 60% load in year one: 48 passengers × $200 = $9,600, minus $9,200, so only $400 per flight. That's $2M of contribution in the first year, not $10M. So in the 12-month window the CEO cares about, redeployment plus the $1.8M of losses we stop gives roughly $3.8M of improvement — contribution around $19.8M against $20M fixed, basically breakeven, not profit.

The connecting traffic worries me too. If 20% of Lakeport and Port Avery passengers connect onward, exiting strips feed revenue off the four healthy routes.

Do we have the revenue attributable to those connecting passengers on the onward legs?

As I mentioned: About 20% of passengers on the two contested routes are connecting at the hub to another Larkspur flight. As the exhibit shows: On the other four routes revenue and contribution stayed nearly flat: Hub–Cedar Bluff (2,500 flights) went from $38.0M to $38.4M of revenue and $5.0M to $5.4M of contribution; Hub–Granite Falls (2,500 flights) from $34.0M to $33.8M and $4.6M to $4.4M; Hub–Millbrook (2,000 flights) from $30.0M to $29.8M and $4.4M to $4.2M; and Hub–Westhaven (2,000 flights) held at $24.8M of revenue and $3.8M of contribution. What else could Larkspur do to make sure it's profitable in the first year?

A few levers, and I'd stack them rather than pick one.

First, phase the exit. Don't drop both routes at once — exit Lakeport first, since it loses $600 a departure versus Port Avery's $200, and redeploy only those 2,000 flights. That caps first-year ramp exposure while keeping Port Avery's feed traffic.

Second, protect the feed. 20% of contested-route passengers connect onward, so exiting costs us onward revenue on the four healthy routes — I'd want that quantified before full exit.

Third, pricing on the four uncontested routes. Nobody has entered there, and contribution margins are thin — Westhaven is $3.6M on $24.8M, under 15%. A $5–10 fare increase there drops almost entirely to contribution and needs no ramp.

Fourth, extras. $20 per passenger is low; bags and seat selection could add $5–8 immediately.

Fifth, revisit the $20M fixed base — it was never scrutinized.

Do we have price elasticity on the four protected routes?

A stacked set of levers. On the price elasticity of those four routes, I'll check what we have. Repeating what I said before: On the other four routes revenue and contribution stayed nearly flat: Hub–Cedar Bluff (2,500 flights) went from $38.0M to $38.4M of revenue and $5.0M to $5.4M of contribution; Hub–Granite Falls (2,500 flights) from $34.0M to $33.8M and $4.6M to $4.4M; Hub–Millbrook (2,000 flights) from $30.0M to $29.8M and $4.4M to $4.2M; and Hub–Westhaven (2,000 flights) held at $24.8M of revenue and $3.8M of contribution. Earlier you mentioned the redeployment swings us by about $13.8M. Can you walk me through the components of that figure?

That figure is stale — it was built on my $8,800 variable cost error. Let me rebuild it.

Two components. One: contribution from the new routes. At full ramp, 56 passengers × $200 revenue per passenger = $11,200, minus $9,200 variable cost = $2,000 per flight, × 5,000 flights = $10M. Two: the losses we stop by exiting. Lakeport is negative $1.2M and Port Avery negative $0.6M, so $1.8M comes back.

$10M plus $1.8M is $11.8M, not $13.8M. I carried the inflated $12M through.

So system contribution at full ramp goes from $16M to $27.8M, less $20M fixed, about $7.8M operating profit. But that's steady state. In year one at 60% load, the new routes earn $400 per flight, $2M total, so contribution is $19.8M — essentially breakeven, which is why the extra levers matter.
Understood. If you had to advise the CEO now, what would you recommend?

My recommendation: exit the two contested routes and redeploy that aircraft time to Ashford and Brookhaven, but phase it and pair it with pricing action so year one isn't a wash.

The why: the entire swing is price, not volume. A low-cost carrier with a 30% cost-per-seat advantage entered Lakeport and Port Avery, we matched fares, and both now lose money on a variable-cost basis — Lakeport $600 a departure, Port Avery $200. We can't win a price war against that cost structure, and fixed costs don't disappear if we simply park the planes.

Redeployment earns about $2,000 per flight at full ramp, roughly $10M of contribution, plus $1.8M of losses stopped — call it $11.8M, taking us to about $7.8M operating profit steady state.

The risk is the ramp: at 60% first-year load that's only $2M, basically breakeven. So I'd exit Lakeport first, raise fares modestly on the four uncontested routes, and lift extras above $20.

Next steps: validate the demand estimates and quantify the 20% connecting-traffic loss.
Understood. What do you see as the single biggest risk to that recommendation, and how would you mitigate it?

The single biggest risk is that the demand estimates for Ashford and Brookhaven don't hold. Everything in the recommendation rests on 70% load at a $180 fare on two routes where nobody flies nonstop today — and "no competitor" can mean untapped demand, or it can mean no one thinks the market is there. If realized load is 60% rather than 70%, contribution per flight falls from $2,000 to $400, an $8M difference. That's the whole swing between a healthy profit and breakeven, and by then we've exited Lakeport and Port Avery and can't easily go back.

Mitigation, in order: validate demand before committing — booking data, connecting volumes through the hub, survey work on those city pairs. Then phase it, as I said: Lakeport's 2,000 flights first, hold Port Avery, and judge the real ramp before moving the rest. And build a trigger — if year-one load trails 65% by month six, redeploy to the four protected routes instead, where Westhaven's $3.6M of contribution shows there's room.
What's the very first thing you'd have the client do?

Before anything structural, I'd have them pull the booking and connecting-traffic data for Ashford and Brookhaven and pressure-test the 70% load, $180 fare planning estimate — that's a two-to-three week exercise using their own hub O&D data plus whatever DOT itinerary data is available, and it gates the entire recommendation.

In parallel, because it costs nothing and needs no ramp, I'd have them implement the extras and fare adjustments on the four uncontested routes immediately — those are protected markets, and Westhaven at $3.6M of contribution on $24.8M of revenue shows how thin the margins are and how much a few dollars per passenger would do.
